explanations.answer: Right into the high priest's courtyard
explanations.explanation: Right into the courtyard, friend. Peter, one of Jesus' followers, stays back at a distance, but he doesn't stop. He walks right in and sits down with the officers. I'd have quit at the first corner and called it a nice evening stroll.

explanations.answer: Only as far as the city walls
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention a city wall. It says Peter follows at a distance, right into the courtyard of the high priest. Peter, one of Jesus' followers, goes all the way in. I think I'd have been the one at the edge holding up a sign saying 'Good luck!'

explanations.answer: Only as far as the Kidron Valley
explanations.explanation: Peter, one of Jesus' followers, doesn't stop partway. The text says he follows right into the high priest's courtyard. He stays back at a distance, but he keeps coming all the way in. The text doesn't mention the Kidron Valley.
Warms is the word. Peter sits with the officers and warms himself by the fire. Just a man at a fire, right in the middle of the officers. I've stood next to my oven the same way, minus the officers.
Hides is a fair guess, but that's not the word the text uses. Peter sits with the officers and warms himself by the fire. Warming is what he's doing there.
The text doesn't say anything about Peter being wet. It says he sits with the officers and warms himself by the fire. Warming is the word. Nobody's hanging laundry in this scene.

Here's what the text really says: the chief priests and the whole Sanhedrin are seeking testimony against Jesus, but they do not find any. They're looking hard and coming up empty. That's the opposite of plenty. It's like walking into a bakery looking for a fresh batch and finding an empty rack.

False is right. The chief priests and the whole Sanhedrin are seeking testimony against Jesus to put Him to death, but they do not find any. They go looking and come back with nothing solid. Not a crumb.

Not quite, friend. The text says many bore false witness against Jesus, but their testimony was inconsistent. The chief priests and the whole Sanhedrin were seeking testimony to put Him to death, but they did not find any. Stories that don't match each other don't give them what they're looking for.
False is right. Many bore false witness against Jesus, but their testimony was inconsistent. Their stories don't line up. That's many witnesses, and still they did not find any testimony.

explanations.answer: Destroy it and build another in three days
explanations.explanation: That's the claim. Some men stand up and testify falsely against Him: “We heard Him say, ‘I will destroy this man-made temple, and in three days I will build another that is made without hands.’…” Then the text adds, “But even their testimony was inconsistent.” So this is what they say, and even it doesn't hold together.

explanations.answer: Tear it down and never build again
explanations.explanation: The men do say Jesus would destroy the temple, but they add something that cuts the other way. They claim He said, “…in three days I will build another that is made without hands.” So no 'never build again' in their story. Building is part of their claim.

explanations.answer: Rebuild it larger over seven years
explanations.explanation: No seven years in this one, friend. The men claim Jesus said He would destroy this man-made temple and in three days build another made without hands. Three days, not seven years.

He stays silent. The text says Jesus remained silent and made no reply. The high priest asks, “Have You no answer?” and still Jesus says nothing. I'll be honest, I couldn't hold quiet through a squeaky drawer.
The text says Jesus remained silent and made no reply. No arguing happens. The high priest even asks, “Have You no answer?” and Jesus says nothing.
The text doesn't show Jesus calling any witnesses. It says He remained silent and made no reply. The witnesses we hear about are the ones testifying against Him, and their testimony was inconsistent.

True. Asked, “Are You the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One?” Jesus says, “I am.” After all that silence, it's a short, plain answer. Then He keeps going: “and you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven.”

Here's what the text says: Jesus answers, “I am.” He doesn't dodge the question or stay silent this time. The high priest asks if He is the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One, and Jesus says yes. Then He keeps going: “and you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven.”
He tears them. The high priest tears his clothes and declares, “Why do we need any more witnesses?” That's a big move in front of the whole council.
The text says the high priest tore his clothes. Taking them off isn't what it says. It happens at this moment, right after Jesus answers.
No ashes here. The text says the high priest tore his clothes and declared, “Why do we need any more witnesses?” Tearing is what he does with his clothes.
Blasphemy is the word. The high priest says, “You have heard the blasphemy. What is your verdict?” That's the charge he puts on the table. And the council takes it from there.
Close, but that's not the word the text uses. The high priest says, “You have heard the blasphemy.” He says it right after he tears his clothes.
Rebellion isn't the word here. The high priest says, “You have heard the blasphemy. What is your verdict?” He names it blasphemy and asks the council to decide.
Here's what the text says: they all condemned Him as deserving of death. The word is all, not some. That's the whole council on one side. It's a heavy moment, friend.
False is right. The text says they all condemned Him as deserving of death. Not some of them, all of them. I think this is a heavy one.

explanations.answer: You were with Jesus the Nazarene
explanations.explanation: That's it. She looks at Peter and says, “You also were with Jesus the Nazarene.” She's one of the servant girls of the high priest. She spots him warming himself by the fire.

explanations.answer: You must be one of the officers
explanations.explanation: She says nothing like that. The servant girl says, “You also were with Jesus the Nazarene.” She connects Peter to Jesus, not to the officers. And Peter had been sitting with those officers.

explanations.answer: You need to leave this courtyard
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't have her telling him to leave. She looks at him and says, “You also were with Jesus the Nazarene.” That's all she says here. It's a simple sentence, but it lands hard.

explanations.answer: He says he doesn't know what she means
explanations.explanation: He denies it. Peter says, “I do not know or even understand what you are talking about…” That's the first of the three denials. It's a hard sentence to read.

explanations.answer: He says yes and asks where Jesus is
explanations.explanation: Peter doesn't say yes. The text says he denied it, “I do not know or even understand what you are talking about…” He doesn't ask about Jesus at all.

explanations.answer: He tells her to go ask the officers
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't show Peter sending her anywhere. He denies it, saying, “I do not know or even understand what you are talking about…” Then he goes out to the gateway.
The rooster crows. Peter goes out to the gateway and the rooster crowed. That's the first crow. Remember it, because it matters later.
The text doesn't mention the fire going out. Peter goes out to the gateway, and then the rooster crowed. Fire's not the answer here, friend.
No slamming gate in this text. When Peter goes out to the gateway, the rooster crowed. That's the sound in the scene.
True. This time the servant girl speaks to those standing nearby, saying, “This man is one of them.” Before, she talked straight to Peter. Now she's telling everyone else around.

Here's what the text says: she saw him again and told those standing nearby, “This man is one of them.” So she does say it, and this time she says it to the people around. It isn't just between her and Peter anymore.
Denies is the word. The text says he denied it again. That's twice now. I think you can hear how hard it's getting for him.
Peter doesn't admit it. The text says he denied it again. That makes it the second time he says no.
Ignoring isn't what the text says. It says Peter denied it again. Denying means saying no, and that's what he does.
Galilean, someone from Galilee. Those standing nearby say, “Surely you are one of them, for you too are a Galilean.” Now they give a reason. The word 'too' is in the text.
Not Samaritan. The people nearby say, “Surely you are one of them, for you too are a Galilean.” A Galilean is someone from Galilee. That's the reason they give.
Moabite isn't in this passage. The people nearby say, “Surely you are one of them, for you too are a Galilean.” Galilean is the word they use.
Here's what the text says: Peter began to curse and swear, “I do not know this man of whom you speak!” He doesn't admit anything. Denial number three. I think this one hurts, friend.
False is right. Peter began to curse and swear, “I do not know this man of whom you speak!” That's the third time he says no. It's the hardest of the three to read.
Three. Peter remembers what Jesus had told him: “Before the rooster crows twice, you will deny Me three times.” Three times is exactly how many it was. Jesus said it, and it happened.
It's three, not four. The word Peter remembers from Jesus is, “Before the rooster crows twice, you will deny Me three times.” Count them in the passage and you get three.
Seven isn't it. Jesus said, “Before the rooster crows twice, you will deny Me three times.” And Peter denies three times. The passage lines up with those words.

He breaks down and weeps. Peter remembers the word Jesus had spoken to him: “Before the rooster crows twice, you will deny Me three times.” I think that's a man whose heart just broke. A sad moment, and an honest one.

explanations.answer: He goes back to the fire
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't send Peter back to the fire. Once he remembers the word that Jesus had spoken to him, he broke down and wept. That's what he does.
The text doesn't say Peter runs anywhere. After he remembers Jesus' words, he broke down and wept. That's the last thing we see him do in this passage.
